summary: Describes experiments involving over 100,000 hosts to evaluate the availability, accuracy, and reliability of time distribution using the Network Time Protocol across the Internet.

eli5.summary: Scientists checked clocks on over a hundred thousand computers to see how well they could all agree on the time.

questions: what is network time protocol accuracy
subtitle: Measured performance of the Network Time Protocol across the Internet with over 100,000 hosts.

tldr.problem: Most Internet hosts have inaccurate clocks set manually and rarely checked, but accurate time is critical for distributed applications.
tldr.mechanism: Large-scale experiments tested NTP and other time protocols on thousands of hosts, measuring accuracy, reliability, and error distributions across diverse Internet paths.
tldr.outcome: NTP maintains time accuracy within tens of milliseconds on most paths, thousands of times better than other protocols, proving it works reliably across the Internet.

today: RFC 1128 documents the measured performance of NTP version 1 and 2 in 1989. NTP has continued to evolve and is still widely used on the Internet for clock synchronization, with current versions offering even better accuracy through improved algorithms and hardware.

sections.title: The Clock Synchronization Problem
sections.content: Most Internet hosts keep time using battery-backed quartz clocks that drift several seconds per day and are checked manually only when they become obviously wrong. A 1988 survey of 5,722 Internet hosts found that 60 percent had errors greater than a minute, and some were off by years. The Network Time Protocol (NTP) was designed to solve this by distributing accurate time automatically across the Internet. This paper describes experiments to measure how well it actually works.
sections.eli5: Computer clocks drift and get wrong. Scientists tested NTP to see if it could keep many computers telling the same time.

sections.title: Large-Scale Testing Across the Internet
sections.content: The experiments surveyed 107,799 distinct Internet hosts, sending time-request messages using three protocols: ICMP Timestamp, TIME, and NTP. Of hosts responding, 20,758 provided valid time indications. A second experiment surveyed NTP primary servers synchronized to national radio standards (WWVB, WWV, and GOES) over a two-week period, collecting about 33,000 samples of roundtrip delay and clock offset. A third set of experiments measured error sources including statistical delays on network paths, radio propagation effects, and radio clock phase noise.
sections.eli5: Researchers sent time questions to thousands of computers and measured how wrong each clock was compared to a reference clock.

sections.title: Accuracy Results
sections.content: NTP hosts maintained median errors of only a few milliseconds, with maximum errors under 50 milliseconds on paths with up to twelve hops. In contrast, ICMP and TIME protocol hosts showed errors ranging from milliseconds to over one day. The experiments demonstrated that NTP is roughly a thousand times more accurate than other protocols. Path delays and radio propagation variations caused the largest errors, but NTP's filtering algorithms successfully removed outliers and maintained stable time.
sections.eli5: NTP was much better than other methods. Most NTP computers were wrong by less than a few thousandths of a second, while others could be off by many minutes or hours.

references.text: Mills, D.L., Network Time Protocol (version 2) specification and implementation, RFC 1119, University of Delaware, September 1989.
